why_here: Emus roam almost every habitat on the mainland, from coastal scrub to the dry interior, following rain to find food.
fun_fact: The male sits on the eggs for about eight weeks, barely eating or drinking the whole time.
clue: A huge flightless bird that can sprint at about 50 km/h. The dad does all the egg-sitting.

why_here: Its giant ears shed heat and pick up prey under the sand, and it can go long spells without drinking.
fun_fact: Its ears can be about 15 cm long, the biggest for its body size of any canid.
clue: A tiny fox with enormous ears that dump heat. It digs dens in sand dunes and rarely drinks.
eco: North Saharan Xeric Steppe and Woodland

why_here: Its long legs suit the tall grass of this vast tropical savanna, where it hunts small animals and eats lots of fruit.
fun_fact: About half its diet is fruit, especially the wolf apple, a tomato relative named after it.
clue: Not a wolf and not a fox: a red, stilt-legged canid that eats nearly as much fruit as meat.

why_here: It thrives in dry open country and can get most of its water from the plants it eats.
fun_fact: When excited it 'pronks', bouncing stiff-legged up to about 2 m into the air.
clue: A gazelle that bounces straight up on stiff legs, about 2 m high, across dry open scrub.

why_here: It is built for sandy deserts: it eats only ants and wicks water from damp sand to its mouth through grooves in its skin.
fun_fact: A single meal can be thousands of ants, picked up one at a time.
clue: A spiky lizard that eats only ants and drinks through grooves in its skin, from damp sand.

why_here: It lives wherever its food trees grow, the eucalyptus woodlands of the east and south-east.
fun_fact: It sleeps up to about 20 hours a day, partly because its leaf diet gives so little energy.
clue: A tree-hugging marsupial that eats almost only eucalyptus and sleeps most of the day.

why_here: Huge herds migrate across one of the last great unfenced grasslands on Earth, chasing fresh grass.
fun_fact: Males grow a swollen throat in the mating season, which gives the species its Latin name.
clue: Herds of up to tens of thousands migrate across endless, unfenced grassland.

why_here: It needs deep, unbroken rainforest, where its striped legs blend into the dappled shade.
fun_fact: It is the giraffe's only living relative and can clean its own ears with its long tongue.
clue: A shy forest animal with zebra-striped legs, the only living relative of the giraffe.

why_here: A great river walls off its forest, which kept its ancestors apart from chimpanzees for about a million years.
fun_fact: Bonobo groups are usually led by females, and they settle tensions with affection rather than fights.
clue: Our closest living relative, along with the chimp, in rainforest walled in by a great river.

why_here: It needs this desert's summer rain and mild winters; a hard frost can kill it.
fun_fact: It may take about 50 to 75 years to grow its first arm.
clue: A giant branching cactus that can take decades to grow its first arm. Frost can kill it.

why_here: It needs this desert's cold winters to flower and depends on one kind of moth to pollinate it.
fun_fact: It is a yucca, not a tree, and only a single moth species pollinates it.
clue: A shaggy, spiky-armed yucca of high desert with cold winters, pollinated by one kind of moth.

why_here: It depends on big, fruiting lowland rainforest trees on one huge island.
fun_fact: It builds a fresh sleeping nest of branches in the treetops almost every night.
clue: A red ape that builds a new treetop nest of branches almost every night, on one big island.

why_here: It grazes high, cold grassland around 3,500 to 5,000 m, where its fine wool keeps it warm.
fun_fact: Its wool is among the finest of any animal, and it is shorn only every few years.
clue: A wild relative of the llama with some of the finest wool on Earth, grazing above 3,500 m.

why_here: It is the only primate that lives mostly on grass, on high plateaus edged by cliffs where it sleeps.
fun_fact: It is sometimes called the bleeding-heart monkey for the red patch of bare skin on its chest.
clue: A grass-eating monkey with a red patch on its chest, sleeping on cliffs of a high plateau.

why_here: The last big wild population of this tiger lives in snowy mixed forests near the Pacific coast.
fun_fact: It is one of the largest cats alive, with a thick coat for winters far below freezing.
clue: The biggest of the big cats, with a thick coat for snowy forest winters far below freezing.

why_here: It is the world's only alpine parrot, living in the mountains and forests of one island.
fun_fact: Kea are famous for pulling apart car wipers, tents and boots out of curiosity.
clue: The world's only alpine parrot, a clever troublemaker that pulls apart car wipers in the snow.
eco: New Zealand South Island montane grasslands
New Zealand South Island temperate forests

why_here: It is adapted to the dry, spiny forest and scrub of the south of one island.
fun_fact: Males hold 'stink fights', wafting scent from their wrists over their tails at rivals.
clue: A striped-tailed primate that holds stink fights, in dry spiny scrub on a big island.

why_here: It lives in cool, misty mountain forest with a thick bamboo understorey, its almost only food.
fun_fact: It eats bamboo for up to about 14 hours a day, using a thumb-like wrist bone to grip it.
clue: A black-and-white bear that eats bamboo up to 14 hours a day in cool, misty mountains.

why_here: It vanished from the mainland thousands of years ago and survives on the island off its south coast.
fun_fact: It has one of the strongest bites for its size of any living mammal.
clue: A stocky black marsupial scavenger with a huge bite for its size, on a cool island.

why_here: It drinks the summer fog that rolls in off the ocean along a narrow coastal strip.
fun_fact: The tallest known living tree, Hyperion, is a coast redwood about 116 m tall.
clue: The tallest trees on Earth, drinking summer fog along a narrow, cool coastal strip.

why_here: It hunts giant mole-rats in Afroalpine moorland above about 3,000 m.
fun_fact: It is Africa's most endangered carnivore, with only about 500 adults left.
clue: A rusty-red wolf that hunts giant mole-rats in cold moorland above about 3,000 m.

why_here: It grows in scattered groves on the western slope of one snowy mountain range.
fun_fact: The General Sherman tree is the largest single tree on Earth by volume.
clue: The bulkiest trees on Earth, in scattered groves on the flank of one snowy mountain chain.

why_here: The last wild cougars in the east of the continent survive in a subtropical swamp and its pine islands.
fun_fact: It nearly vanished, down to about 20 to 30 animals in the 1990s, before a rescue plan.
clue: The last wild cougars of their side of the continent, hunting deer in a subtropical swamp.

why_here: It survives on coastal fog in one of the driest deserts on Earth.
fun_fact: It grows only two leaves in its whole life, which can last over a thousand years.
clue: A plant with just two leaves for its whole life, living on fog in a coastal desert.

why_here: It lives in the canopy of wet evergreen hill forest along one mountain chain.
fun_fact: It has a silver-white mane around its face and a tufted tail like a lion's.
clue: A black monkey with a silver mane and a tufted tail, high in wet hill forest.
eco: South Western Ghats moist deciduous forests
South Western Ghats montane rain forests

why_here: It lives only in the wet eastern rainforest of one big island and dies quickly in captivity.
fun_fact: It is the largest living lemur, and its eerie songs can carry about 2 km.
clue: The biggest lemur of all, whose eerie songs carry about 2 km through wet forest.

why_here: Shea grows wild in the long band of wooded grassland from Senegal to Uganda, where farmers leave the trees standing in their fields.
fun_fact: A shea tree can take 15 years or more to bear its first fruit, and it may keep fruiting for two centuries.
clue: Its nuts give a creamy butter used in skin creams and chocolate.

why_here: It strides across the open grassy country south of the Sahara, from Senegal to Ethiopia, hunting on foot.
fun_fact: It does almost all its hunting on the ground, catching lizards, snakes and even small mammals with its huge bill.
clue: A big black bird that walks rather than flies, with a casque on its bill and bare blue skin.

why_here: Sable are specialists of the miombo woodlands, grazing in grassy clearings close to water and cover.
fun_fact: The giant sable, a rare form found only in Angola, is a national symbol there.
clue: Glossy black males carry long horns that sweep back like scimitars.

why_here: Grey parrots live in the lowland forests of the Congo Basin and the Gulf of Guinea, roosting in big noisy flocks.
fun_fact: A grey parrot named Alex learned over 100 words and could name colours and shapes.
clue: A grey bird with a bright red tail, famous for copying human speech.

why_here: Meerkats need open dry ground with firm soil for digging burrows, which the Kalahari and Karoo have in plenty.
fun_fact: Meerkats are fairly resistant to scorpion venom and teach their pups how to handle stinging prey.
clue: One stands up on its back legs as a lookout while the rest of the gang digs for food.

why_here: Gemsbok can go for long spells without drinking, so they roam the driest parts of Namibia, Botswana and South Africa.
fun_fact: A gemsbok can let its body heat up during the day instead of sweating, which saves precious water.
clue: Straight horns up to a metre long and a bold black and white face mask.

why_here: The gerenuk browses the thorny bush of Somalia, Ethiopia, Kenya and northern Tanzania, where few grazers can compete with it.
fun_fact: Gerenuks get almost all their water from the leaves they eat and may never need to drink.
clue: This long-necked antelope stands up on its hind legs to nibble leaves out of reach.

why_here: This viper lives across the sand seas and stony plains of the Sahara, hiding in the sand by day.
fun_fact: It shuffles itself into loose sand until only its eyes and horns poke out, then waits for prey.
clue: A sidewinding snake with a little spike over each eye.
eco: North Saharan Xeric Steppe and Woodland

why_here: These gorillas live in the lowland and swamp forests of Gabon, Cameroon, Congo and nearby countries.
fun_fact: Almost all gorillas in zoos are western lowland gorillas.
clue: A great ape whose family troops are led by a big male with a silver back.

why_here: This raven is found only in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea, often around farms and villages.
fun_fact: It is one of the biggest songbirds in the world, rivalling the common raven in size.
clue: A huge black bird with a deep, arched bill and a white patch on the back of its neck.

why_here: The fossa hunts in forests all around Madagascar, the only place it lives.
fun_fact: It looks like a cat but is more closely related to mongooses.
clue: A sleek hunter that climbs trees head first and preys on lemurs.

why_here: This sifaka lives in the dry spiny and gallery forests of southern and southwestern Madagascar.
fun_fact: On the ground it moves by bouncing sideways on its back legs, which looks like dancing.
clue: A white leaper with a dark cap that crosses open ground in sideways hops.

why_here: Blesbok are grazers of the open high grasslands of South Africa's interior plateau.
fun_fact: Its name comes from the Afrikaans word for the white blaze down its face.
clue: A reddish antelope with a white stripe running down its whole face.

why_here: It feeds in short, often burnt high grassland in South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, and nests on cliffs nearby.
fun_fact: It likes freshly burnt grass because insects are easy to spot there.
clue: A glossy green-black bird with a bare white face and a bright red crown.

why_here: It lives on the rugged hills and gravel plains along the edge of the Namib in Namibia and southwest Angola.
fun_fact: It can dig holes in dry riverbeds to reach water, which other animals then use.
clue: A striped horse with a white belly, a fold of skin on its throat and nimble hooves for rocks.

why_here: The Nile lechwe lives only in the great Sudd marshes of South Sudan and the nearby Machar marshes.
fun_fact: Males turn dark chocolate brown with a bright white patch on the shoulders.
clue: An antelope that wades into knee-deep water to graze, with long backswept horns.

why_here: Tommies live on the short grass plains of Kenya and northern Tanzania, following the rains with the big herds.
fun_fact: When chased, it leaps stiff-legged into the air, a move called stotting.
clue: A small, fast gazelle with a bold black stripe along each side.

why_here: Pygmy hippos live along streams in the lowland forests of Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea and Ivory Coast.
fun_fact: A baby pygmy hippo named Moo Deng became an internet star in 2024.
clue: A shy, pig-sized cousin of a much bigger river animal.

why_here: It nests on boulders and rock overhangs in the forests of Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast and Ghana.
fun_fact: It glues its cup-shaped mud nest straight onto the face of a rock.
clue: A bald bird with a bright yellow head that hops about rocks instead of flying far.

why_here: It lives on the mountain slopes of Yemen and southwest Saudi Arabia, where seasonal rains keep plants green.
fun_fact: It drinks by lapping up dew and raindrops from leaves rather than from standing water.
clue: A popular pet lizard with a tall crest on its head shaped like a helmet.
eco: Southwest Arabian Escarpment shrublands and woodlands
Southwest Arabian montane woodlands and grasslands

why_here: It lives in the humid forests of eastern and northern Madagascar.
fun_fact: It is one of the heaviest chameleons in the world and can live for decades.
clue: One of the biggest of its kind, about the length of a forearm, with a green or turquoise body.

why_here: It lives only in the dry spiny forest of southern Madagascar.
fun_fact: Tu'i Malila, said to be a gift from Captain Cook to Tonga's royal family, was a radiated tortoise and lived to about 188.
clue: Each plate of its high-domed shell has yellow lines bursting out like a star.

why_here: It forms dense thickets in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, where it is the main plant of the Albany thicket.
fun_fact: Elephants love to eat it, and people plant it to soak up carbon.
clue: A succulent shrub with small round leaves, a favourite snack of elephants.

why_here: The last wild asses live in the hot, rocky Danakil lowlands of Eritrea and Ethiopia, near the Horn of Africa.
fun_fact: It is the wild ancestor of the domestic donkey.
clue: A tough grey wild horse relative with zebra-like stripes on its legs.

why_here: It lives on the dunes of the Namib, where morning fog rolls in from the cold sea.
fun_fact: It climbs a dune crest, tips its head down and lets fog collect on its back and run into its mouth.
clue: This beetle does a headstand on misty mornings to drink.

why_here: Drills live only in the forests between the Cross River in Nigeria and the Sanaga River in Cameroon, plus Bioko.
fun_fact: Drill groups sometimes join together into gatherings of more than 100 animals.
clue: A short-tailed monkey with a black face and a bright red lower lip.

why_here: This monkey lives only between the Niger and Cross rivers in southeastern Nigeria.
fun_fact: Some villages treat the monkeys as sacred and protect them in their groves.
clue: A rare little monkey with a white spot on its nose and a pale throat.

why_here: The beira lives on dry, rocky hills in northern Somalia and nearby Djibouti and Ethiopia.
fun_fact: It gets most of its water from plants and can go without drinking.
clue: A small, sure-footed antelope with very large ears for its size.

why_here: It lives among rocky outcrops on the Jos Plateau of central Nigeria.
fun_fact: It was only described as a new species in 1998.
clue: A tiny red finch that went unnoticed by science until the late 1990s.

why_here: This monkey is found only in the swamp forests of the Niger Delta in Nigeria.
fun_fact: It eats mostly leaves and has a stomach with several chambers to digest them.
clue: A leaf-eating monkey with no thumbs and a rusty red coat.

why_here: It grows in the dry spiny forest of southwestern Madagascar, the only place it lives.
fun_fact: It belongs to the Didiereaceae, a plant family found only on Madagascar.
clue: A spiny plant whose thorny arms reach up and wave like tentacles.

why_here: Lions need open grassland and woodland full of grazing animals, and the savannas of East and southern Africa hold the biggest herds.
fun_fact: A lion's roar can be heard up to about 8 kilometers away.
clue: The only big cat that lives in family groups, called prides.

why_here: Giraffes browse the tops of acacia and other trees scattered across the open bushlands of East and southern Africa.
fun_fact: A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as a human.
clue: The tallest animal alive, with a dark tongue about half a meter long.

why_here: Plains zebras graze tough grasses and need water nearby, which the grasslands and woodlands from Kenya to South Africa provide.
fun_fact: No two zebras have exactly the same pattern of stripes.
clue: A wild horse in black and white stripes, every coat one of a kind.

why_here: Elephants roam the woodlands and bushlands of East and southern Africa, with the largest herds in Botswana, Zimbabwe, Tanzania and Kenya.
fun_fact: It is the largest land animal on Earth, and an adult can eat over 100 kilograms of plants a day.
clue: The heaviest land animal, it uses its trunk to smell, drink, and say hello.

why_here: Hippos spend the day in rivers and lakes and come out at night to graze, so they live where water meets grassland, from the Nile swamps to the Zambezi.
fun_fact: Hippos cannot really swim; they walk or bounce along the bottom of rivers.
clue: A huge animal that hides in water all day and comes out at night to eat grass.

why_here: Chimps live in the forests of central and West Africa, mostly north of the Congo River, where fruit trees grow all year.
fun_fact: Chimpanzees make and use tools, such as stripping twigs to fish termites out of mounds.
clue: Our closest living relative, along with the bonobo. It fishes for termites with twigs.

why_here: Cheetahs hunt by sprinting, so they need wide open ground, and most of the world's wild cheetahs live in Namibia, Botswana, Kenya and Tanzania.
fun_fact: A cheetah can go from standstill to about 100 km/h in around three seconds.
clue: The fastest land animal, with black tear marks running down its face.

place: East and southern Africa's open country
why_here: Ostriches roam dry, open plains where they can see danger coming and outrun it, from the Kalahari and Karoo to the plains of Kenya and Tanzania.
fun_fact: Its eye is bigger than its brain.
clue: The biggest bird in the world. It cannot fly but can run about 70 km/h.

why_here: Wildebeest follow the rains to fresh short grass, most famously in the Serengeti and Masai Mara.
fun_fact: Calves can stand and run within minutes of being born.
clue: Over a million of these gnus march in a giant loop each year, chasing fresh grass.

place: East and southern Africa's dry savannas
why_here: Baobabs grow in hot, seasonally dry savannas, storing water in their trunks to get through the long dry season.
fun_fact: Some baobabs have been dated at over 1,000 years old.
clue: A tree with a fat, water-storing trunk that looks like it was planted upside down.

why_here: Asian elephants need big forests with grass and water, found in India's hills and the forests of Myanmar, Thailand and the rest of Southeast Asia.
fun_fact: Unlike African elephants, usually only some Asian elephant males grow tusks.
clue: Smaller-eared than its cousins, it has worked alongside people for thousands of years.
eco: South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests
South Western Ghats moist deciduous forests

why_here: Snow leopards hunt wild sheep and goats on steep, rocky slopes high in the Himalaya, Tibet, the Pamirs and the Tian Shan.
fun_fact: It wraps its long, thick tail around its face like a scarf to keep warm.
clue: A smoky-gray big cat of high cliffs that cannot roar and uses its tail as a scarf.
eco: Eastern Himalayan alpine shrub and meadows
North Tibetan Plateau-Kunlun Mountains alpine desert
Tian Shan montane steppe and meadows
Tibetan Plateau alpine shrublands and meadows
Western Himalayan alpine shrub and meadows

why_here: King cobras hunt other snakes in the warm, wet forests of mainland Southeast Asia and northeast India.
fun_fact: It is the only snake known to build a nest for its eggs.
clue: The world's longest venomous snake. It mostly eats other snakes.

why_here: Bactrian camels handle the Gobi's scorching summers and freezing winters, and herders across Mongolia and northern China still raise them.
fun_fact: Its humps store fat, not water.
clue: Two humps, a shaggy winter coat, and it can drink about 100 liters in minutes.

why_here: Dromedaries were first tamed in Arabia, and they are still part of life across its sandy and stony deserts.
fun_fact: It can lose about a quarter of its body water and still be fine.
clue: The one-humped camel, with bushy eyelashes and nostrils it can close against sand.
eco: South Arabian plains and plateau desert

why_here: Reindeer, called caribou in North America, graze lichen on the cold, treeless tundra all around the Arctic, and many are herded by peoples such as the Sámi and Nenets.
fun_fact: It is the only deer where both males and females grow antlers.
clue: The only deer where females grow antlers too. Some pull sleighs for herders.
eco: Scandinavian Montane Birch forest and grasslands

why_here: Hedgehogs like hedges, woodland edges and gardens full of beetles and worms, which are common across western Europe and Britain.
fun_fact: An adult hedgehog has around 5,000 to 7,000 spines.
clue: A small night-time garden visitor that rolls into a spiky ball when scared.
eco: Northeast Spain and Southern France Mediterranean forests

why_here: White storks nest on rooftops and poles in farm country across Europe, with big numbers in Spain, Poland and the Baltic states.
fun_fact: Storks have no voice box, so they greet each other by clattering their bills.
clue: A tall white bird that nests on chimneys and is said to deliver babies.

why_here: Red squirrels live in conifer and mixed forests where they can feed on pine and spruce seeds, from Spain and Britain across to Siberia.
fun_fact: It buries food in many hidden stores and forgets some, which helps new trees grow.
clue: A rusty-orange tree climber with tufted ears that grow longer in winter.

why_here: This oak grows in deep, damp lowland soils across most of Europe, from Ireland and France to Ukraine.
fun_fact: A single old oak can support hundreds of kinds of insects.
clue: Its acorns dangle on long stalks, and its leaves have little ear-like lobes at the base.

why_here: Red deer live in woods, moors and hills across Europe, from the Scottish Highlands and Spain to the Carpathians.
fun_fact: A stag grows a new set of antlers every year.
clue: In autumn the stags roar and clash antlers to win mates.

why_here: Polar bears hunt seals on the sea ice and rest and den on the cold coasts and islands around the Arctic Ocean, and about two thirds of them live in Canada.
fun_fact: Its fur looks white, but its skin underneath is black.
clue: The largest land meat-eater. It hunts seals from floating ice.

why_here: Grizzlies need big wild country with berries, roots and salmon, which is why most live in Alaska, the Yukon, British Columbia and the northern Rockies.
fun_fact: In late summer some grizzlies eat up to about 40,000 moths a day to fatten up for winter.
clue: A brown bear with a big shoulder hump and long claws for digging.

why_here: Moose browse willows and water plants in the cold northern forests and wetlands that stretch from Alaska across Canada to Maine.
fun_fact: Moose are strong swimmers and can dive to eat plants from lake bottoms.
clue: The biggest deer on Earth, with wide flat antlers and a flap of skin under its chin.

place: Alaska, Canada and the Great Lakes
why_here: Bald eagles catch fish, so they nest near coasts, rivers and lakes, and the biggest numbers live in Alaska, British Columbia and the lake country of Canada and the northern US.
fun_fact: Its nest can weigh over a ton after years of being added to.
clue: A national bird that isn't bald: its white head feathers just look that way from afar.

why_here: Raccoons thrive in woods near water and in towns, and they are especially common in the forests and farmland of the eastern and central US.
fun_fact: Its front paws are so sensitive that it often feels for food underwater instead of looking.
clue: A masked, ring-tailed night raider famous for opening trash cans.

why_here: Beavers need streams and plenty of aspen, willow and birch to eat and build with, which the forests of Canada and the northern US have in abundance.
fun_fact: Its front teeth are orange because they contain iron, which makes them tougher.
clue: A flat-tailed builder that dams streams to make its own ponds.

place: The Great Plains and Great Basin
why_here: Pronghorn need wide open grass and sagebrush country where speed keeps them safe, with Wyoming at the heart of their range.
fun_fact: It is the fastest land animal in its part of the world, able to run around 90 km/h.
clue: Not a true antelope, yet it can outrun almost anything over long distances.

why_here: Wild turkeys feed on acorns, nuts and seeds in the oak forests and clearings of the eastern and central US.
fun_fact: Wild turkeys can fly short bursts at around 80 km/h and roost in trees at night.
clue: A big bird with a bare head that changes color when it gets excited. Gobble gobble.

why_here: Coyotes do well in open plains and dry scrub, and the West's grasslands and deserts are their original heartland.
fun_fact: Coyotes have spread so widely that they now live in big cities like Los Angeles and Chicago.
clue: A wild dog famous for its night-time yips and howls, and for chasing a roadrunner.

place: The central and eastern United States
why_here: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, which grows across the prairies and farm country of the US Midwest and East where monarchs breed each summer.
fun_fact: Eastern monarchs fly up to about 4,000 km to spend winter in the mountains of central Mexico.
clue: An orange and black butterfly that flies thousands of km south each autumn.

why_here: Jaguars hunt along rivers and wetlands in big forests, and the Amazon and the Pantanal are their strongholds.
fun_fact: Jaguars have one of the strongest bites of any cat and often kill by biting through the skull.
clue: A spotted big cat that loves to swim and hunts caimans.

why_here: This three-toed sloth spends its life high in the trees of the warm, wet Amazon forests, eating leaves.
fun_fact: Algae grows in its fur and gives it a greenish tint that helps it hide.
clue: It moves so slowly that algae grows in its fur, and it climbs down only to poop.

why_here: Anacondas spend most of their time in slow rivers, swamps and flooded forests, which cover huge areas of the Amazon and the Llanos of the Orinoco.
fun_fact: It is the heaviest snake in the world, and big females can top 100 kilograms.
clue: The world's heaviest snake, a swamp-dwelling constrictor that can swallow a deer.

why_here: Capybaras graze near water and escape danger by diving in, so they gather in the wetlands of the Pantanal, the Llanos and the rivers of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay.
fun_fact: It can stay underwater for about five minutes to hide from predators.
clue: The world's biggest rodent, a calm swimmer that other animals like to sit on.

why_here: Giant anteaters roam open grasslands dotted with termite mounds, which are everywhere in the Cerrado, Pantanal and Llanos.
fun_fact: Its tongue can flick in and out about 150 times a minute.
clue: No teeth, but a sticky tongue about 60 cm long that slurps up 30,000 ants a day.

why_here: Wild cacao trees grow in the shade of the warm, humid forests of the upper Amazon, where the plant first evolved.
fun_fact: Its pods grow straight out of the trunk, and each holds dozens of seeds.
clue: Its bitter seeds, once used as money, are the start of every chocolate bar.

why_here: Brazil nut trees rise above undisturbed Amazon forest, where the bees that pollinate them and the agoutis that spread their seeds live.
fun_fact: The nuts grow inside a hard, coconut-sized pod that holds about 10 to 25 of them.
clue: Giant trees whose nuts come packed in a pod as hard as a cannonball.

why_here: Condors soar on rising winds along the Andes and over the open plains of Patagonia, searching for dead animals to eat.
fun_fact: It can glide for hours, and one was recorded flying over 170 km without flapping.
clue: One of the biggest flying birds, a vulture with a wingspan over 3 meters.

why_here: Eastern greys graze in grassy woodlands and forest edges across the wetter eastern side of Australia, from Queensland to Victoria.
fun_fact: A big male can stand taller than an adult person.
clue: A big hopping grazer that carries its joey in a pouch. Not the red one.

why_here: Echidnas live almost anywhere with ants and termites to eat, and they are common across the woodlands and forests of eastern Australia.
fun_fact: A baby echidna is called a puggle.
clue: A spiny ant-eater that lays eggs, one of only a handful of mammals that do.

why_here: Wild budgies roam Australia's dry interior in big flocks, following rain to find grass seeds and water.
fun_fact: Wild budgies are almost always green and yellow; blue and other colors come from captive breeding.
clue: A little green and yellow parrot, wild in huge flocks, kept as a pet all over the world.

why_here: Red kangaroos live across the dry open plains of inland Australia, where they graze on grass that springs up after rain.
fun_fact: It is the largest living marsupial, and a big male can clear about eight metres in a single bound.
clue: The biggest pouched animal alive, it can't walk backwards and uses its tail as a fifth leg.

why_here: Kookaburras need open woodland with big old trees for nest hollows, which runs down the whole east of Australia.
fun_fact: Its loud call, often heard at dawn, sounds so much like human laughter that it is used in old jungle films.
clue: A giant kingfisher that eats snakes and lizards, and whose call sounds like loud laughter.

why_here: Frilled lizards live in the warm, grassy woodlands across the top of Australia, spending most of their time up trees.
fun_fact: When scared it opens a wide frill around its head, hisses, then runs away on its back legs.
clue: When scared it flares a huge collar of skin, gapes its mouth, then sprints off on two legs.

why_here: This dragon basks on logs and fence posts across the dry woodland and scrub of inland eastern and southern Australia.
fun_fact: It waves one arm in a slow circle to signal that it is not a threat to a bigger lizard.
clue: A spiky-chinned lizard that puffs out a dark throat when cross, and is a popular pet worldwide.

why_here: Peafowl live in the open forests, farmland and scrub found almost everywhere across the plains and plateaus of India.
fun_fact: The male's long train is not his tail but very long back feathers, each with an eye pattern.
clue: The male fans out about 200 shimmering feathers covered in eye spots to impress females.

South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests
South Western Ghats moist deciduous forests
South Western Ghats montane rain forests

why_here: Chital graze in the open deciduous forests and grassy clearings that cover much of India.
fun_fact: Chital often follow troops of langur monkeys, eating fruit they drop and listening for their alarm calls.
clue: A deer with a coat of white spots it keeps all its life, and a favourite meal of tigers.
eco: Central Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests
North Western Ghats moist deciduous forests
South Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests
South Western Ghats moist deciduous forests
Upper Gangetic Plains moist deciduous forests

why_here: Platypuses need clean rivers and creeks with banks to dig burrows in, found along the wet eastern side of Australia and in Tasmania.
fun_fact: It finds food with its eyes shut, sensing the tiny electric signals from the muscles of shrimp and worms.
clue: An egg-laying mammal with a duck-like bill and venom spurs on the male's back legs.

why_here: Lyrebirds scratch for insects in the damp leaf litter of the tall wet forests from Victoria to southern Queensland.
fun_fact: It can copy almost any sound it hears, from other birds to camera shutters and chainsaws.
clue: A ground bird famous for perfectly mimicking other birds, car alarms and even chainsaws.

why_here: The boab grows on the rocky plains and sandy soils of the Kimberley and nearby Victoria River country, where wet and dry seasons alternate.
fun_fact: One hollow old boab near Derby is said to have been used as a lockup for prisoners.
clue: Its fat bottle-shaped trunk stores water, and it loses all its leaves in the dry season.

why_here: It lives only in the cool, mossy mountain forests along New Guinea's central range.
fun_fact: The male's two head plumes can be twice as long as his body and are worn in local headdresses.
clue: The male grows two head plumes longer than his body, each lined with little blue flags.
eco: Central Range Papuan montane rain forests

why_here: It walks the floor of the lowland and swamp forests along the north of New Guinea.
fun_fact: It is about the size of a turkey, making it one of the largest pigeons in the world.
clue: A turkey-sized pigeon wearing a lacy crest of blue feathers tipped with white.
eco: Northern New Guinea lowland rain and freshwater swamp forests

why_here: The last tigers of the Sunda islands hunt in Sumatra's forests, from coastal peat swamps up into the mountains.
fun_fact: It is the smallest living tiger, with darker fur and narrower stripes than tigers on the mainland.
clue: The smallest of its kind, with stripes so close together they sometimes merge.

why_here: These tigers roam the forests of Peninsular Malaysia and the far south of Thailand.
fun_fact: It appears on Malaysia's coat of arms and is the national animal.
clue: A big striped cat that stands on a national coat of arms, though fewer than 200 are left.

why_here: Blackbuck graze the open grasslands and dry scrub of western and peninsular India.
fun_fact: Blackbuck can run at about 80 km per hour and leap high into the air while fleeing.
clue: The male is nearly black on top with long spiral horns, and can sprint at 80 km per hour.
eco: Central Deccan Plateau dry deciduous forests

why_here: This kiwi probes the soft forest floor for worms and grubs across the native forests of New Zealand's North Island.
fun_fact: Its egg is about a fifth of the mother's body weight, one of the largest eggs for a bird its size.
clue: A flightless night bird with nostrils at the tip of its long bill, laying a giant egg.
eco: New Zealand North Island temperate forests

why_here: Maleos live in the lowland and hill forests of Sulawesi and walk to warm beaches or volcanic soil to lay their eggs.
fun_fact: Chicks hatch fully feathered, dig themselves out of the sand and can fly the same day.
clue: Buries its eggs in sun-warmed sand or hot volcanic soil, then leaves the heat to hatch them.

why_here: Nearly all the remaining birds live on the dry open grasslands of the Thar in Rajasthan.
fun_fact: It is one of the heaviest flying birds, and power lines are now one of its biggest dangers.
clue: One of the heaviest birds that can still fly, standing about a metre tall.

why_here: It travels in noisy groups through the tall lowland forests of Borneo, the only place it lives.
fun_fact: It is so unusual that scientists place it in a bird family all of its own.
clue: A crow-sized bird with a bare red head topped by stiff bristles, the only one in its family.

why_here: Nilgiri tahr graze the high grassy hilltops and cliffs of the southern Western Ghats.
fun_fact: Eravikulam National Park in Kerala holds the largest herd, and they are often seen beside the road.
clue: A stocky wild goat that lives on steep cliffs, the only one of its kind in its home country.
eco: South Western Ghats montane rain forests

why_here: Most of these rhinos live on the grassy floodplains of the Brahmaputra in Assam, with Kaziranga holding the largest herd.
fun_fact: Its thick skin has folds that make it look like it is wearing a suit of armour.
clue: A one-horned giant whose folded skin looks like plates of armour.

why_here: The wild ass lives on the flat salt plains of the Little Rann of Kutch and grazes on the grassy patches around it.
fun_fact: It can run at about 70 km per hour and keep up a fast pace over long distances.
clue: A sandy-coloured wild relative of the donkey that grazes on salt flats in the heat.
eco: Rann of Kutch seasonal salt marsh

why_here: This gibbon lives only in the remaining forests of western and central Java, high in the canopy.
fun_fact: Females sing the loud morning songs that mark the family's territory.
clue: A silvery-grey ape that swings arm over arm through the canopy and sings at dawn.

why_here: Saola live only in the wet forests of the Annamite Mountains on the border of Laos and Vietnam.
fun_fact: It was unknown to science until 1992 and has been photographed in the wild only a handful of times.
clue: A shy forest ox nicknamed a unicorn, first described by scientists only in 1992.

why_here: This magpie lives in the broadleaf forests on Taiwan's hills and low mountains.
fun_fact: Family groups help raise each brood, and they will dive at people who come too close to a nest.
clue: A long-tailed blue bird with a red bill that was voted a national bird in 2007.

why_here: Kauri grows only in the warm north of New Zealand's North Island, north of about 38 degrees south.
fun_fact: The largest living kauri, Tāne Mahuta, has a trunk over 4 metres wide.
clue: A giant conifer with column-like trunks, whose old fossil gum was dug up for varnish.

why_here: This flightless bird lives on grassy ground near water across Tasmania.
fun_fact: It can run at about 50 km per hour, using its short wings for balance.
clue: A flightless chicken-sized bird with a lime-green bill that can sprint fast.

why_here: The kagu lives on the floor of the humid forests of Grande Terre in New Caledonia.
fun_fact: It has flaps covering its nostrils, which no other bird has, to keep out dirt while it digs.
clue: A pale grey, nearly flightless bird that raises a big crest and barks like a dog.

why_here: This cockatoo lives in the lowland forests of Seram and a few small nearby islands in the Moluccas.
fun_fact: It has one of the loudest calls of any parrot, and its bite can crack big nuts.
clue: A pale peach parrot with a big salmon-pink crest it fans out when excited.

why_here: It lives only in the remaining forest on Sumba, where it eats figs and other fruit.
fun_fact: Like other hornbills, the female is sealed inside a tree hole with mud while she nests.
clue: A big black bird with a ridged bill that nests in tree holes sealed with mud.

why_here: It lives on the floor of the lowland forests of Palawan in the Philippines.
fun_fact: The male shows off by spreading his tail and tilting it so the blue eye spots catch the light.
clue: The male has a metallic blue crest, a white eyebrow and a tail full of eye spots.

why_here: Karri needs deep soil and high rainfall, found only in the far southwest corner of Western Australia.
fun_fact: Some karri trees once had fire lookout platforms built near the top, which visitors can still climb.
clue: One of the tallest hardwood trees on Earth, with smooth bark that peels to pale cream.

why_here: The last wild takahē were found in the Murchison Mountains of Fiordland, where they graze on alpine tussock.
fun_fact: It was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in 1948.
clue: A chunky flightless bird with a huge red bill, thought extinct until 1948.

why_here: It lives in the wet forests and tussock high country of northwest Nelson, the northwest of New Zealand's South Island.
fun_fact: It is the largest kiwi and can live in cold, snowy places up to 1,500 metres.
clue: The biggest of its kind, a flightless night bird of cold, snowy hills.

why_here: It lives only in the wet forests of southwest Sri Lanka, from the lowlands into the hills.
fun_fact: It often joins mixed flocks of other birds as they move through the forest.
clue: A bright blue bird with a chestnut head and a red bill and eye ring.

why_here: It follows the snowshoe hare, which lives across the spruce forests of Canada and Alaska.
fun_fact: Its numbers rise and crash on a roughly ten-year cycle that tracks the hares it eats.
clue: Its huge furry paws work like snowshoes, and it lives mostly on one kind of hare.

why_here: Tens of millions once grazed the grasslands of the Great Plains, from Alberta down to Texas.
fun_fact: It is the national mammal of the United States and can run at about 55 km/h.
clue: The heaviest land animal of its home range, it rolls in dust baths called wallows.

why_here: It needs short grass where it can see predators coming, so it digs its towns across the dry western plains.
fun_fact: One colony in Texas was said to cover about 65,000 square kilometres and hold millions of animals.
clue: This chubby squirrel lives in burrow 'towns' and greets family with a kiss.

why_here: It thrives in the cold winters and rich soils of the Great Lakes, New England and the St. Lawrence valley.
fun_fact: It takes about 40 litres of sap to boil down to one litre of syrup.
clue: Its sap becomes pancake syrup, and its leaf is on a famous red and white flag.
eco: Gulf of St. Lawrence lowland forests

place: The Gulf and southern Atlantic coastal plain
why_here: It needs warm, slow fresh water, which the swamps and rivers of the southeastern coastal plain have plenty of.
fun_fact: The temperature of the nest decides whether the eggs hatch as males or females.
clue: Its snout is broad and U-shaped, and it can go through thousands of teeth in a lifetime.

place: The Chihuahuan, Sonoran and Mojave deserts
why_here: It hunts lizards, snakes and insects across the hot, dry scrublands of the US Southwest and northern Mexico.
fun_fact: It can run at about 30 km/h and will kill and eat rattlesnakes.
clue: A ground-running cuckoo that a cartoon made famous for saying 'beep beep'.

why_here: It grows on the sandy, fire-swept coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and the Gulf.
fun_fact: Young trees spend years in a 'grass stage' that looks like a tuft of grass and survives fire.
clue: Frequent fires help this tree, and it once covered about 360,000 square kilometres.

why_here: It digs its burrows in the deep sandy soils under the longleaf pines of the Southeast.
fun_fact: Its burrows give shelter to more than 350 other kinds of animals.
clue: Its burrow can be 3 m deep and 12 m long, and hundreds of species move in.

why_here: It spends most of its life underground in the Sonoran Desert, coming out mainly after spring and summer rains.
fun_fact: A compound from its saliva led to a diabetes drug called exenatide.
clue: A slow, beaded orange and black lizard with a venomous bite and a fat tail.

why_here: It survives the Mojave's heat by spending most of the year in burrows.
fun_fact: It can store water in its bladder and go a year or more without drinking.
clue: It can live 50 years or more and spends up to 95% of its life underground.

why_here: It eats almost nothing but sagebrush in winter, so it lives where the sagebrush sea grows.
fun_fact: Males puff up two yellow air sacs on their chests that pop loudly when they display.
clue: In spring, males strut on dancing grounds called leks, popping air sacs on their chests.

place: California's Central Valley and oak foothills
why_here: It lives only in California, in the oak savannas and farmland of the Central Valley and nearby hills.
fun_fact: It is one of very few bird species found only in California.
clue: A long-tailed black and white crow relative with a bright yellow bill.

place: The mountains of Alaska and the Yukon
why_here: It lives on steep alpine slopes in the mountains of Alaska, the Yukon and the Mackenzie Mountains.
fun_fact: Rams' curled horns grow a ring each year, so you can count their age.
clue: This all-white wild sheep has amber curled horns and climbs steep cliffs to escape wolves.

why_here: It is the signature plant of the Chihuahuan Desert, so common that its range is used to map that desert.
fun_fact: Its tough leaf fibre, called ixtle, has long been used for brushes and rope.
clue: Its stiff, spiky leaves can puncture tyres and boots, and its fibre makes brushes.

why_here: It forms the pinyon-juniper woodlands that cover the mesas of the Colorado Plateau.
fun_fact: Pinyon jays bury its seeds by the thousands and forget some, planting new trees.
clue: Its tasty nuts were a key food for many Native peoples and are still gathered in autumn.

why_here: This small elk evolved in the grasslands and tule marshes of California's Central Valley.
fun_fact: It fell to perhaps a handful of animals in the 1870s and has recovered to several thousand.
clue: The smallest elk of its kind, named after a marsh plant, it once nearly vanished.

why_here: It nests only in the oak and Ashe juniper woods of central Texas, using juniper bark for its nest.
fun_fact: It is the only bird that breeds only in Texas.
clue: This little songbird builds its nest from strips of juniper bark and nests in one state.

why_here: It is adapted to the tall coastal grasslands along the Gulf coast of Texas and Louisiana.
fun_fact: Only a small wild flock survives, kept going by captive breeding and releases.
clue: Males inflate orange neck sacs and boom at dawn to win mates.

why_here: It rings the Central Valley in the dry foothills of California's Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada.
fun_fact: In a drought it can drop all its leaves in summer to save water.
clue: Its leaves have a bluish tint, and it can drop them in summer to survive drought.

why_here: It grows only in the wet mountains of southwest Oregon and northwest California.
fun_fact: Its fragrant wood was so prized in Japan that logs were shipped there for temples and coffins.
clue: Garden forms of this tree, called Lawson cypress, are planted all over the world.

why_here: It grows almost only in the Vizcaíno region of central Baja California.
fun_fact: It was named after a creature in Lewis Carroll's poem 'The Hunting of the Snark'.
clue: It looks like an upside-down carrot and is named after a creature in a Lewis Carroll poem.

why_here: It lives only in cold, clear, rocky streams of the Ozarks in Missouri and Arkansas.
fun_fact: It breathes mostly through the wrinkly folds of skin along its sides.
clue: A giant salamander up to 60 cm long, nicknamed the 'snot otter'.

why_here: It lives only in the coastal sage scrub of southern California and northern Baja California.
fun_fact: Its call sounds like a kitten's mew.
clue: This tiny grey songbird mews like a kitten and depends on coastal sage scrub.

why_here: It lives in the deep loess soils of the Palouse hills of eastern Washington and Idaho.
fun_fact: It was long rumoured to smell like lilies, but recent finds did not back that up.
clue: This rare pale worm can be close to a metre long and was once thought lost.

why_here: It grows in the bare, wind-carved 'blowouts' of the Nebraska Sand Hills.
fun_fact: It was once thought to be one of the rarest plants on the Great Plains.
clue: Its pale blue flowers smell of vanilla, and it grows in bowls blown out by wind.

why_here: Its caterpillars feed on Kincaid's lupine, which grows in the Willamette Valley's remnant grasslands.
fun_fact: It was thought extinct for over 50 years until it was found again in 1989.
clue: This small blue butterfly was lost for decades and depends on one kind of lupine.

why_here: This black bear subspecies lives in the wet coastal forests of central and northern British Columbia.
fun_fact: In some places up to one in ten is born white thanks to a recessive gene, yet it is not an albino.
clue: A black bear that is sometimes born creamy white, and fishes for salmon in daylight.

why_here: It grows on rocky slopes across the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts of the US Southwest and northern Mexico.
fun_fact: It can grow a full set of leaves within days of a rain and drop them again when it dries out.
clue: Its whip-like spiny stems look dead most of the year, then leaf out days after rain.

why_here: It lives among granite rocks and snowmelt in the high Sierra Nevada of California.
fun_fact: It can curl into a ball and roll downhill to escape danger.
clue: This flat-headed salamander has webbed toes for clinging to wet granite near snowfields.

why_here: This big flightless bird needs wide open grassland and scrub, which stretches from central Brazil down through the Chaco to the Pampas of Argentina and Uruguay.
fun_fact: The males build the nest, sit on eggs laid by several females, and raise the chicks alone.
clue: A flightless giant where dads incubate up to 50 eggs from several mothers.

place: Patagonia and the high southern Andes
why_here: Guanacos graze dry, cold, open country, from the Patagonian plains up into the arid high Andes of Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru.
fun_fact: It is the wild ancestor of the llama and can spit when annoyed.
clue: The wild ancestor of the llama, it can spit at rivals when annoyed.

why_here: It swims the rivers and seasonally flooded forests of the Amazon basin, where high water lets it hunt fish among the drowned trees.
fun_fact: Its neck bones are not fused, so it can turn its head to steer around tree trunks.
clue: A pink dolphin that weaves between flooded tree trunks to catch fish.

why_here: Unlike most toucans it likes semi-open woodland, so it thrives in the Cerrado, Pantanal and nearby dry forests of central South America.
fun_fact: Its huge bill is light and hollow, and it helps the bird shed body heat.
clue: The biggest of its family, with a bright orange bill that works like a radiator.

why_here: It stalks open grassland and dry scrub across central and eastern South America, from the Caatinga and Cerrado to the Chaco.
fun_fact: It kills lizards and snakes by grabbing them in its bill and smashing them on the ground.
clue: A long-legged hunter with a loud yelping call that beats prey against rocks.

why_here: Colonies dig big burrow systems in the flat grasslands and scrub of Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia.
fun_fact: It piles sticks, bones and other odd objects around the entrances of its burrows.
clue: A chunky rodent with a striped face that decorates its burrow with collected junk.

why_here: It lives in the wet forests of the upper Amazon in Ecuador, Peru, Colombia and far western Brazil, often near flooded river edges.
fun_fact: It is one of the smallest monkeys in the world and weighs about as much as a stick of butter.
clue: One of the world's tiniest monkeys, it gnaws holes in bark to drink tree sap.

why_here: It is found only in the thorny dry scrub of the Gran Chaco in Paraguay, Bolivia and Argentina, where it eats cacti and bromeliads.
fun_fact: Scientists knew it only from fossils until living animals were found in 1975.
clue: Known only from fossils until living herds turned up in 1975.

why_here: It lives mainly in the Caatinga, the dry thorn scrub of northeastern Brazil, and digs for ants and termites.
fun_fact: It was the mascot of the 2014 FIFA World Cup.
clue: It rolls into a perfect ball, and it was a World Cup mascot in 2014.

why_here: It is found only in Argentina, in the open dry scrub of the Monte and the plains of Patagonia.
fun_fact: Mara pairs often stay together for life.
clue: A rodent with long legs like a small deer that hops and gallops like a hare.

place: The Araucaria highlands of southern Brazil
why_here: This conifer dominates the cool, misty highland forests of southern Brazil and nearby Argentina, which are named after it.
fun_fact: Its big edible seeds, called pinhão, are roasted and sold as a winter snack.
clue: Its candelabra shape and big edible seeds make it a winter snack favourite.

why_here: This holly grows wild in the humid inland forests where Paraguay, northeast Argentina and southern Brazil meet.
fun_fact: Its leaves are brewed into a caffeine-rich drink sipped through a metal straw.
clue: A holly whose dried leaves are sipped from a gourd through a metal straw.

why_here: This tiny deer hides in the dense, rainy temperate forests of southern Chile and nearby Argentina.
fun_fact: It stands only about 40 cm tall at the shoulder.
clue: One of the world's smallest deer, barely knee high, with tiny spiky antlers.

why_here: It is found only in central Chile, living in burrow colonies in the dry shrubland between the Andes and the coast.
fun_fact: Unlike most rodents, it is active by day and can see ultraviolet light.
clue: A social pet rodent that is awake by day and sees ultraviolet light.

why_here: It lives in the rivers and lagoons of the Orinoco basin, which wind across the Llanos grasslands of Venezuela and Colombia.
fun_fact: It is one of the largest crocodiles in the world, with males reaching over 5 m.
clue: A huge crocodile with a long, narrow snout and one of the rarest on Earth.

why_here: Huge numbers gather in the seasonal wetlands of the Pantanal and the Paraguay River basin, where floods bring plenty of fish.
fun_fact: Its jagged lower teeth poke up through holes in its top jaw, which earned it the nickname piranha caiman.
clue: Nicknamed after a famous toothy fish because its lower teeth stick up over its lip.

why_here: It feeds in the salty lakes of the high puna where Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina meet.
fun_fact: It is the only flamingo with yellow legs.
clue: The only flamingo with yellow legs, it filters tiny algae from salty lakes.

why_here: It lives only in the forests of the Yucatán Peninsula, including parts of Belize and northern Guatemala.
fun_fact: Its tail feathers have blue-bronze eyespots like a peacock's.
clue: A turkey with peacock-like eyespots on its tail and a bumpy blue head.

why_here: It nests on rocky outcrops and cliffs in the forests of the Guiana Shield, across the Guianas, southern Venezuela and northern Brazil.
fun_fact: Males gather at display grounds called leks and show off to visiting females.
clue: A bright orange bird with a half-moon crest that hides its own bill.

why_here: It lives only in the coastal Atlantic Forest of eastern Brazil, from Bahia to Espírito Santo.
fun_fact: It has a mane of long dark hair on its neck and shoulders.
clue: A slow mover with a dark mane on its neck and shoulders.

why_here: It is native to the Pampas of Argentina and Uruguay, where it often stands alone on the flat grassland as the only shade for miles.
fun_fact: It is not really a tree but a giant herb with soft, spongy wood.
clue: Looks like a huge tree, but it is really a giant herb with soft wood.

why_here: It is found only on Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud.
fun_fact: It is the smallest bird in the world, weighing less than 2 grams.
clue: The smallest bird in the world, lighter than a dime.

why_here: It survives only on Hispaniola, shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.
fun_fact: It is one of the few mammals with venomous saliva, delivered through grooved teeth.
clue: A shrew-like mammal with a long snout and a venomous bite.

why_here: It lives in the steep coastal Atlantic Forest of the Serra do Mar in southeastern Brazil.
fun_fact: Muriquis are famous for being peaceful and often hug each other.
clue: The largest monkey of its region, known for hugging instead of fighting.

place: The Caribbean side of Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama
why_here: It lives in the wet lowland forests on the Caribbean side of Nicaragua, Costa Rica and western Panama.
fun_fact: Mothers carry each tadpole to its own tiny pool and feed it unfertilised eggs.
clue: A tiny red frog with blue legs, like it is wearing jeans.

place: The Pacific coast of Costa Rica and Panama
why_here: It is found only in the wet forests along the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and western Panama.
fun_fact: Troops can have dozens of monkeys moving noisily through the trees together.
clue: A small orange-backed monkey with a black cap and a white mask.

why_here: This hummingbird lives only on Jamaica, where it is the national bird.
fun_fact: Locals call it the doctor bird because its black crest and long tail look like an old doctor's top hat and coat.
clue: Called the doctor bird, the male trails two long streamer tail feathers.

why_here: This little frog is native to Puerto Rico, where its night chorus is part of daily life.
fun_fact: It skips the tadpole stage, and baby frogs hatch straight from the eggs.
clue: A tiny frog named after its two-note call, "ko-KEE", heard all night.

place: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
why_here: It is found only in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, a lone coastal mountain range in northern Colombia.
fun_fact: Its home mountains rise from the sea to snow peaks in only about 42 km.
clue: A yellow songbird with a bold black-and-white striped head and a very tiny home range.

place: The Chocó of Colombia and Ecuador
why_here: It lives only in the very wet lowland and foothill forests of the Chocó, on the Pacific side of Colombia and Ecuador.
fun_fact: It looks almost identical to the bigger yellow-throated toucan, and the two are easiest to tell apart by their calls.
clue: A yellow-bibbed bird with a two-tone bill, best told from its lookalike cousin by its croak.

why_here: It is found only in the lowland forests of northwestern Colombia, between the Atrato and Magdalena rivers.
fun_fact: Older siblings help carry and care for the twins born in each family group.
clue: A tiny monkey with a wild crest of white hair, like a punk rock hairdo.

why_here: It lives in the cold cloud forests and high páramo grasslands of the Andes in Colombia, Ecuador and northern Peru.
fun_fact: It is the only tapir with a thick woolly coat, which keeps it warm at high altitude.
clue: The only one of its kind with a thick woolly coat, plus a short bendy trunk.

why_here: It lives in the dry coastal strip west of the Andes in Peru and southwest Ecuador, from sand dunes to dry forest.
fun_fact: In dry spells it can get by on seeds and pods alone and may go without drinking.
clue: The smallest of its fox family, it can survive on seed pods and very little water.

place: The dry forests of western Mexico
why_here: It lives in the seasonal dry forests along Mexico's Pacific side, from Jalisco south to Oaxaca and inland in the Balsas basin.
fun_fact: It is one of very few venomous lizards, and compounds from its relative's venom led to a diabetes drug.
clue: A venomous lizard with bead-like scales, a close cousin of the Gila monster.

why_here: It lives in the high cloud forests of the Sierra Madre de Chiapas and nearby volcanoes in Guatemala.
fun_fact: It is the only living species in its genus and is thought to be an ancient branch of its family.
clue: A big black bird with a bright red horn sticking straight up from its head.
eco: Sierra Madre de Chiapas moist forests

why_here: This giant cactus grows only in the dry Tehuacán-Cuicatlán valley of Puebla and Oaxaca in central Mexico.
fun_fact: Near its tip it grows a woolly patch of golden hairs on one side, where the flowers appear.
clue: A tall unbranched column cactus named after a famous carved column in Rome.

place: The Chang Tang and Kunlun plateaus
why_here: It grazes the cold, high grasslands of the Chang Tang and Hoh Xil, mostly above 4,000 metres, where few people live.
fun_fact: Its underfur, called shahtoosh, led to heavy poaching because one shawl needed the wool of several animals.
clue: Its wool is so fine that a whole shawl made from it can be pulled through a ring.
eco: North Tibetan Plateau-Kunlun Mountains alpine desert

why_here: It is the main tree of the huge forests east of the Yenisei, rooting in the thin layer of soil above permafrost.
fun_fact: It is one of the most northerly trees on Earth, growing past 72°N on the Taimyr Peninsula.
clue: A conifer that drops all its needles each autumn and grows on ground frozen year-round.

place: The taiga from Scandinavia to the Yenisei
why_here: This big grouse needs old conifer forest with a berry-rich floor, which runs unbroken across northern Europe and western Siberia.
fun_fact: In winter it lives almost entirely on pine needles.
clue: The world's largest grouse. Males click, pop and gurgle at dawn displays called leks.

why_here: It hunts voles and eats pine nuts and berries in the dense conifer forests that cover Siberia from the Urals to the Pacific.
fun_fact: The hunt for its fur drove Russia's push east across Siberia in the 1600s.
clue: Its silky fur was once paid as tax to the tsars.

why_here: It thrives where summers are mild and rain falls all year, from France and Germany into the Alps, Carpathians and Dinaric hills.
fun_fact: Its shade is so deep that few plants can grow on the floor of an old beech wood.
clue: Smooth grey bark, and nuts called mast that feed boars and jays in bumper years.

why_here: It digs burrows in the dry clay and sand plains of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan to escape the heat and the cold.
fun_fact: It may be active for only about three months a year, spending the rest asleep in its burrow.
clue: Two of these were among the first animals to fly around the Moon, in 1968.

why_here: It digs big burrow colonies in the open grasslands of Mongolia, Inner Mongolia and Transbaikalia.
fun_fact: In Mongolia it is traditionally cooked by filling its body with hot stones, a dish called boodog.
clue: A chunky burrower that whistles alarms, sometimes cooked with hot stones inside it.

why_here: It lives on steep, rocky slopes above the tree line across the Alps, from France to Austria.
fun_fact: By the early 1800s only about 100 were left, in Italy's Gran Paradiso, and all of today's ibex descend from them.
clue: Huge curved horns, and it climbs near-vertical dam walls to lick the salt.

why_here: It nests in big trees in the open oak woodlands and scrub of central and southwestern Spain and Portugal, where rabbits are plentiful.
fun_fact: It fell to about 30 pairs in the 1960s and has since recovered to several hundred pairs.
clue: Bright white shoulder patches, and a diet that is mostly rabbit.
eco: Southwest Iberian Mediterranean sclerophyllous and mixed forests

why_here: It needs cold, fast, clean mountain streams, found in the Pyrenees and the mountains of northern Spain and Portugal.
fun_fact: It finds prey underwater by touch, using a long, bendy snout covered in sensitive organs.
clue: A tiny swimmer with a trunk-like snout, a close cousin of moles.

place: Manchuria and the Russian Far East
why_here: It is the key tree of the mixed forests of northeast China, Primorye and North Korea.
fun_fact: Its big seeds are one of the main kinds of pine nut sold around the world.
clue: Its cones never open, so nutcrackers, squirrels and boars break in for the seeds.

why_here: It grows on cool, snowy mountain slopes from Turkey's Taurus range south to Mount Lebanon.
fun_fact: It is the tree shown on the flag of Lebanon.
clue: A tree on a national flag, prized in ancient times for temples and ships.
eco: Southern Anatolian montane conifer and deciduous forests

why_here: It grazes the high, dry grasslands of the Tibetan Plateau, from Ladakh across the Chang Tang.
fun_fact: It is the largest of the wild asses, standing about 1.4 metres at the shoulder.
clue: The biggest wild ass, grazing at over 4,000 metres.

why_here: It lives in cold mountain forests of central China, getting through snowy winters on lichen and bark.
fun_fact: It has a bright blue face and a nose so short it is little more than two nostrils.
clue: Blue face, golden fur, and a nose turned up so far it seems to be missing.

why_here: It is the main tree of the open oak woodlands that cover the Zagros Mountains of Iran and Iraq.
fun_fact: Villagers in the Zagros once ground its acorns into flour for bread.
clue: Mountain villagers once baked bread from the acorns of this tree.

why_here: It forms wild fruit forests on the slopes of the Tian Shan in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Xinjiang.
fun_fact: It is the main wild ancestor of the apples sold in shops today.
clue: The wild ancestor of the fruit in your lunchbox, still growing in mountain forests.
eco: Tian Shan montane steppe and meadows

why_here: It lives in cool, damp mountain meadows and forests of the Alps and the Dinaric ranges, where there is little open water.
fun_fact: It gives birth to fully formed young, so it never needs a pond.
clue: Jet black, it gives birth to live young after a pregnancy of two to four years.

why_here: It lives only in flooded caves of the limestone karst running from Slovenia through Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.
fun_fact: It can live for over 100 years and survive for years without eating.
clue: A blind, pink cave amphibian once thought to be a baby dragon.

why_here: It grows wild only in the damp Hyrcanian forests along the southern Caspian shore of Iran and Azerbaijan.
fun_fact: Its leaves turn red, orange and gold in autumn, so it is planted in gardens around the world.
clue: A witch-hazel cousin with flaking bark and some of the best autumn colour of any tree.

why_here: It lives only on the steep, rocky slopes of the Hajar Mountains of Oman and the UAE.
fun_fact: It needs to drink often, so it stays within reach of mountain springs.
clue: A small wild goat cousin that clambers over sheer, sun-baked rock.
eco: Al-Hajar foothill xeric woodlands and shrublands

why_here: It lives along shady, mossy streams in the wet hills of Galicia, northern Portugal and Asturias.
fun_fact: Like a lizard, it can drop its tail to escape a predator.
clue: A slim amphibian with two gold back stripes that drops its tail like a lizard.

why_here: It lives in cold, clear mountain streams and lakes of the Pyrenees in France, Spain and Andorra.
fun_fact: During courtship the male wraps his tail around the female to hold her.
clue: A rough-skinned newt of icy streams; males hug their mates with their tails.

why_here: It grows on the dry plains and hills of southwest Morocco, where its deep roots survive long droughts.
fun_fact: Goats climb high into its branches to eat the fruit.
clue: Goats climb into its branches to eat the fruit, and its kernels give a prized oil.
eco: Mediterranean Acacia-Argania dry woodlands and succulent thickets

why_here: This wild goat lives in the rugged mountains and gorges of Crete, such as the Samaria Gorge.
fun_fact: Its ancestors may have been goats brought by early farmers thousands of years ago.
clue: A shy wild goat of rocky gorges, shown in ancient Minoan art.

why_here: This wild sheep lives in the forested Troodos and Paphos hills of Cyprus.
fun_fact: It appears on the Cypriot 1, 2 and 5 cent euro coins.
clue: A wild sheep pictured on the smallest coins of its home.

why_here: It roams the cold, empty high plateau of northern Tibet and Qinghai, where its thick coat handles temperatures far below freezing.
fun_fact: A big bull can stand about 2 metres at the shoulder and weigh around a tonne.
clue: A shaggy wild ox whose long skirt of hair nearly sweeps the ground.
eco: North Tibetan Plateau-Kunlun Mountains alpine desert
Tibetan Plateau alpine shrublands and meadows

why_here: It digs burrows in short grassland on the plains of Hungary, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria and nearby lowlands.
fun_fact: It hibernates for up to six months a year in its burrow.
clue: A sandy-coloured burrower that stands upright to watch for hawks, then whistles.

why_here: Britain's last wildcats hang on in the forest edges and moors of the Scottish Highlands, after being wiped out further south.
fun_fact: It looks like a big tabby, but its thick tail has blunt black rings and a rounded black tip.
clue: Looks like a chunky tabby, but its bushy tail ends in a blunt black tip. Untameable.

why_here: It evolved in the high-altitude lake system of the Valley of Mexico, and the Xochimilco canals are the last remnant of that ancient lake water.
fun_fact: Axolotls usually never undergo metamorphosis, keeping their feathery external gills and aquatic life as adults.
clue: It usually never grows up: adults keep feathery gills and live in the canals of a high lake.

why_here: It has been trapped in a single water-filled limestone cavern since the region dried out, and it breeds on one small sunlit rock shelf near the surface.
fun_fact: Its whole wild range is a single pool, often called the smallest range of any vertebrate on Earth.
clue: Its whole wild range is one pool in a desert cave, often called the smallest of any vertebrate.

why_here: Sloths on this small island were cut off from the mainland by rising seas and shrank in size over thousands of years of isolation.
fun_fact: Its entire world sits on an island of only about 4 square kilometres, and many live in red mangroves along the shore.
clue: Shrunk by isolation, it lives on an island of about 4 square km, often in red mangroves.

place: Ilha da Queimada Grande (Snake Island), Brazil
why_here: Rising sea levels isolated its ancestors on a small offshore island with no ground prey, so it adapted to hunting migratory birds.
fun_fact: Its venom is reported to be several times more potent than that of its mainland relative, the jararaca.
clue: With no ground prey on its tiny island, this viper ambushes migrating birds instead.

place: Upper Gulf of California near San Felipe, Mexico
why_here: This porpoise is confined to the warm, shallow, murky waters at the very northern end of the Gulf of California.
fun_fact: It is the world's most endangered marine mammal; 2025 surveys identified only around 7 to 10 individuals.
clue: The world's smallest porpoise. Only about 10 are left, in warm, murky water at a sea's far end.

place: Mountains of central Vancouver Island, British Columbia
why_here: It descends from marmots isolated on Vancouver Island's subalpine meadows after the last ice age.
fun_fact: Its chocolate-brown coat with a white nose patch sets it apart from every other marmot.
clue: Chocolate-brown with a white nose patch, it whistles from subalpine meadows on a big island.

why_here: Glaciers and lowland forest cut its meadows off from other marmots, leaving it isolated on the Olympic Peninsula's peaks.
fun_fact: Schoolchildren campaigned for years to get it named Washington's official endemic mammal in 2009.
clue: Glaciers stranded it on peak meadows; kids campaigned for years to make it a state emblem.

place: Santa Cruz Island, Channel Islands, California
why_here: Its ancestors reached a single Channel Island and have evolved there in isolation for about a million years.
fun_fact: It is the only land bird in the continental US that lives on just one island.
clue: Bigger and bluer than its mainland kin, it buries acorns on one hilly isle, alone for ages.

place: Cypress Point and Point Lobos, Monterey Peninsula, California
why_here: It is a relict of cooler times that survives only on two foggy headlands near Carmel.
fun_fact: Though planted worldwide, its entire native range is just two small coastal groves.
clue: Planted worldwide, yet wild only in two small groves on foggy, windswept headlands.

why_here: It depends on high-altitude bunchgrass meadows that exist only on a few volcanoes southeast of Mexico City.
fun_fact: Like pikas, and unlike other rabbits, it gives high-pitched calls to warn others of danger.
clue: A tiny, short-eared rabbit of high bunchgrass meadows that squeaks alarm calls like a pika.

why_here: Raccoons isolated on Cozumel evolved into a separate, much smaller species.
fun_fact: They have been seen rolling paper into balls as toys, a habit learned within family groups.
clue: A dwarf raccoon from a tropical island, seen rolling paper into balls to play with.

why_here: This hummingbird diverged from mainland relatives after colonizing Cozumel's forests.
fun_fact: Males sport a long, deeply forked tail that looks like a pair of scissors.
clue: A glittering hummingbird of island forests; males sport a long tail forked like scissors.

why_here: It evolved on a small Pacific island off Colombia, separated from mainland anoles.
fun_fact: Both males and females are entirely blue, a color that is extremely rare in lizards.
clue: Males and females alike are all blue, a rare colour for a lizard, on one small rainy island.

why_here: It needs the spring-fed gallery forests on the slopes of one plateau surrounded by dry caatinga.
fun_fact: It was not discovered until 1996, and part of its core breeding area lies inside a water theme park.
clue: Unknown until 1996, it needs spring-fed forest on a dry plateau; some breed in a water park.

why_here: It is tied to forest edges and scrub in one Andean valley system in northern Peru.
fun_fact: Males have only four tail feathers, two of which end in large racket-shaped discs they wave during courtship.
clue: Males have just four tail feathers, two tipped with rackets they wave in a mountain valley.

why_here: Its ancestors rafted to Grand Cayman and evolved in isolation in the island's dry shrubland.
fun_fact: It fell to fewer than 15 wild animals in 2003 and recovered to hundreds thanks to captive breeding.
clue: Fewer than 15 were left in the wild in 2003; breeding brought this dry-scrub lizard back.

why_here: Mongooses and development wiped it out elsewhere in Jamaica, leaving only the rugged dry limestone forest of Hellshire.
fun_fact: It was thought extinct until a hunter's dog chased one into a hollow log in 1990.
clue: Thought extinct until 1990, when a hunter's dog chased one into a log in dry limestone scrub.

why_here: This nearly flightless grebe evolved on a single high Andean lake and never leaves it.
fun_fact: It lives at over 4,000 m elevation and its fate depends on water levels controlled by a hydroelectric dam.
clue: Nearly flightless, it never leaves one lake over 4,000 m up, its level set by a hydro dam.

why_here: It is adapted to the cold, oxygen-poor water of the Titicaca basin and breathes mostly through its skin.
fun_fact: Its baggy, heavily folded skin increases surface area for absorbing oxygen; Cousteau's team filmed one 120 m deep.
clue: Baggy, folded skin soaks up oxygen in a cold, high lake; one was filmed 120 m deep.

place: Sulphur Mountain hot springs, Banff, Alberta
why_here: It lives only in the warm, sulphur-rich outflows of a handful of hot springs on one mountainside.
fun_fact: It thrives in water with so much hydrogen sulfide and so little oxygen that most animals could not survive.
clue: A tiny snail of warm, smelly hot-spring runoff on a mountainside, where little else survives.

place: Edwards Aquifer at San Marcos, Texas
why_here: It lives permanently in the dark, water-filled caves of one section of the Edwards Aquifer.
fun_fact: It has no functional eyes and no skin pigment, yet can regrow lost limbs and tail.
clue: Eyeless and ghost-white, it lives in flooded caves underground and can regrow lost limbs.

why_here: It depends on the constant cool spring water flowing out of the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer.
fun_fact: Its species name comes from Austin's Save Our Springs ordinance.
clue: It keeps its frilly gills for life, in a single spring that stays cool all year round.

place: Coastal plain around Wilmington, North Carolina
why_here: It needs fire-maintained, nutrient-poor wet savannas found only in a small part of the Carolinas coastal plain.
fun_fact: A trap only snaps shut after two touches of its trigger hairs within about 20 seconds.
clue: A trap snaps only after two touches within about 20 seconds, in fire-swept, boggy savanna.

why_here: It is an ice-age relict that survived in the cool, shaded ravines along the Apalachicola River.
fun_fact: It was once so common that settlers cut its trunks into planks to build a riverside village.
clue: An ice-age relict conifer of cool, shady river ravines, once common enough to saw for planks.

place: Santa Lucia Mountains, Big Sur, California
why_here: It survives in fire-sheltered canyons and rocky slopes of the Big Sur coast range.
fun_fact: It is the rarest fir in North America, with spiky cones bristling with long needle-like bracts.
clue: The rarest fir on its continent, with spiky cones, in fire-sheltered canyons above the sea.

why_here: It is a relict of ice-age lakes and rivers that once filled the Owens Valley.
fun_fact: In 1969 the entire known population was carried to safety in two buckets.
clue: A relict of ice-age desert lakes. Its whole known population was once saved in two buckets.

place: Hawksbill, Stony Man and The Pinnacles, Shenandoah NP, Virginia
why_here: It clings to cool, rocky talus slopes on three peaks where competitors are scarce.
fun_fact: It has no aquatic larval stage; babies hatch from eggs on land as tiny salamanders.
clue: No water stage: babies hatch on land, on cool, rocky talus slopes of only three peaks.

why_here: It lives only in the spring-fed marshes of an isolated desert basin.
fun_fact: Unlike other box turtles it is mostly aquatic, spending about 90% of its time in water.
clue: Unlike its kin it is mostly aquatic, spending about 90% of its time in desert spring marsh.

why_here: Like the axolotl, it evolved to stay aquatic in a single high-altitude Mexican lake.
fun_fact: Nuns at a local convent have run a breeding program for it for years.
clue: Nuns at a convent breed this gilled, lifelong-aquatic amphibian from one high-altitude lake.

place: Isla Santa Catalina, Gulf of California, Mexico
why_here: It evolved in isolation on a single small desert island in the Gulf of California.
fun_fact: It is a rattlesnake with no rattle: the tail tip breaks off at each shed.
clue: No rattle here: the tail tip breaks off at each shed. It hunts on one small desert island.

why_here: It survives only in a fog-fed grove high on the north end of a remote Pacific island.
fun_fact: Its fruits are edible, which is where the name edulis comes from; goats nearly destroyed it before being removed.
clue: Its fruit is edible. It survives in a fog-fed grove on a remote island once ravaged by goats.

why_here: It evolved on a remote volcanic island far off Mexico's Pacific coast.
fun_fact: It was once placed in its own genus until DNA showed it is a true Mimus mockingbird.
clue: Once given a genus of its own until DNA showed its kin, it lives on a remote volcanic isle.

why_here: It is specialized for the mangrove forests of one small Caribbean island.
fun_fact: Its hatchlings are born dark rather than green, camouflaging them on the mangrove floor.
clue: Its hatchlings are dark, not green, hiding them on the mangrove floor of one small island.

why_here: Its ancestor reached this remote Pacific island and evolved there rather than in the Galápagos.
fun_fact: It is the only one of Darwin's finches that lives outside the Galápagos.
clue: Each bird picks its own speciality, nectar or insects or seeds, on one rainy, forested isle.

why_here: It lives only on the slopes of one volcano at the north end of Isabela.
fun_fact: Rangers first noticed the pink iguanas in 1986, but they were only named as a species in 2009.
clue: Pink with dark bands, it lives on just one volcanic slope, and was named a species in 2009.

why_here: Rich cold upwelling waters off the western Galápagos let it feed without flying, and there were no land predators to escape.
